title: American Pragmatism: Peirce, James and Dewey
subtitle: What difference would it make? America's homegrown philosophy of ideas that work
objectives: By the end you will be able to describe the Transcendentalist background of Emerson and Thoreau and explain why pragmatism both grew from it and broke with it
State Peirce's pragmatic maxim and use it to test whether a dispute is real or merely verbal
Explain William James's theory of truth and his argument in 'The Will to Believe,' including W.K. Clifford's opposing view
Describe John Dewey's vision of education as experience and democracy as a way of life
Weigh the strongest objections to pragmatism, especially the charge that it confuses truth with usefulness
hook:
A camping party in the mountains, sometime in the 1890s. While the others are off on a walk, a squirrel clings to one side of a tree trunk, and a man stands on the opposite side trying to see it. He moves quickly around the tree, but the squirrel moves just as quickly in the same direction, always keeping the trunk between them. The question that sets the campers arguing: does the man go *round* the squirrel? He goes round the tree, and the squirrel is on the tree. But he never gets to its back or its front, because it always faces him.

William James, who tells this story at the start of the second lecture in his book *Pragmatism* (1907), was asked to settle the quarrel. His answer was simple. It depends on what you practically *mean* by "going round." If you mean passing from north of the squirrel to east, south and west of it, then yes. If you mean being first in front of it, then behind it, then in front again, then no. Make the distinction and there is nothing left to argue about. That little trick, asking what practical difference a claim makes, is the heart of **pragmatism**, the first philosophical movement born in the United States. Today we meet its three founders, and the restless American thinkers who came before them.

sections.heading: Before Pragmatism: Emerson, Thoreau and the American Scholar
sections.body:
Until the mid-nineteenth century, American intellectual life mostly borrowed from Europe. The first serious attempt at an independent voice came from a group in and around Concord, Massachusetts, known as the **Transcendentalists**, who believed that intuition could grasp truths transcending the senses. Their leader was Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882), a former Unitarian minister who left the pulpit to become a lecturer and essayist.

In his essay *Nature* (1836) Emerson presented the natural world as a symbol of spirit and urged his readers to have "an original relation to the universe" instead of seeing it through the eyes of dead generations. In his 1837 Harvard address "The American Scholar," which Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. later called America's intellectual Declaration of Independence, he told Americans to stop listening so reverently to the courtly muses of Europe. And in "Self-Reliance" (1841) he preached trust in one's own thought: "Whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist," and, famously, "A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds."

His younger friend Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862) put self-reliance into practice. From 1845 to 1847 he lived in a small cabin he built at Walden Pond, on land Emerson owned, to see what life required when stripped to its essentials; *Walden* (1854) is the result. In 1846 he spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax to a government that supported slavery and the Mexican–American War. The essay that came out of it, now known as "Civil Disobedience" (1849), later inspired Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. Remember Socrates in prison (Day 10), refusing to escape because he respected the laws? Thoreau gives the opposite answer: conscience comes before the law.

Why start here? Because the pragmatists inherited the Transcendentalists' confidence that Americans could think for themselves, their focus on the individual's lived experience, and their impatience with abstract European systems. William James's family knew Emerson well, and James later gave a centenary address in his honor. But the pragmatists replaced mystical intuition with something tougher: the experimental method of modern science, and the shock of Darwin.

sections.heading: The Metaphysical Club and Peirce's Pragmatic Maxim
sections.body:
In 1872, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, a handful of young men began meeting to argue about philosophy. They half-jokingly called themselves the **Metaphysical Club**. Among them were the future Supreme Court justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., the young doctor and psychologist William James, and a brilliant, difficult scientist named Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914; his surname is pronounced like "purse").

Peirce was a polymath: a chemist, astronomer, mathematician and logician who worked for decades for the US Coast and Geodetic Survey. In two essays for *Popular Science Monthly*, "The Fixation of Belief" (1877) and "How to Make Our Ideas Clear" (1878), he laid out what became pragmatism.

He began with a psychological observation. **Doubt** is an uneasy, irritating state; **belief** is a calm and satisfactory one, and a belief is essentially a habit of action. Inquiry is the struggle to get from doubt to belief. Peirce compared four ways of "fixing" belief. The method of *tenacity* is clinging to what you already think and avoiding contrary evidence. The method of *authority* lets an institution decide for everyone. The *a priori* method accepts whatever seems "agreeable to reason." Only the method of *science* lets beliefs be settled by something outside us, by reality itself, through tests that anyone can repeat. It is the only method that can correct its own mistakes.

Then came the famous **pragmatic maxim**, from "How to Make Our Ideas Clear": "Consider what effects, that might conceivably have practical bearings, we conceive the object of our conception to have. Then, our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object." In plain English: if you want to know what an idea means, ask what difference it would make in experience if it were true. If two theories predict exactly the same experiences in every possible situation, they do not really differ.

Peirce also insisted that all our knowledge is provisional, a view he called **fallibilism**. Science does not begin from certain foundations, as Descartes hoped (Day 43); it is a community of inquirers who gradually correct one another. He defined truth as the opinion that would eventually be agreed upon by everyone who investigated long enough.

Peirce's life was not a happy one. His abrasive manner and a scandal around his divorce and remarriage cost him his only university post, at Johns Hopkins, in 1884. He spent his last decades poor and isolated in Milford, Pennsylvania, writing tens of thousands of pages that went largely unpublished in his lifetime. When James made "pragmatism" famous, Peirce disliked what his friend had done with it and renamed his own version **pragmaticism**, a word, he said, ugly enough to be safe from kidnappers.

sections.heading: William James: Truth That Happens to Ideas
sections.body:
William James (1842–1910) came from a remarkable family; his brother was the novelist Henry James. He trained as a doctor, taught anatomy and physiology at Harvard, and wrote *The Principles of Psychology* (1890), a founding text of modern psychology that gave us the phrase "stream of consciousness." In 1898, in a lecture at Berkeley, he introduced pragmatism to the public, generously crediting Peirce for the idea. His lectures published as *Pragmatism* (1907) made it a sensation. He dedicated the book to the memory of John Stuart Mill (Day 61), from whom, he wrote, he first learned the pragmatic openness of mind.

James used the pragmatic maxim as Peirce had, to dissolve empty disputes like the squirrel case. But he applied it far more broadly, including to the idea of truth itself. What is it for a belief to be true? The traditional answer is **correspondence**: a true belief matches reality. James did not deny this, but he asked what "agreement with reality" amounts to in practice. His answer: true ideas are those we can assimilate, validate, corroborate and verify. They lead us successfully through experience. A true belief about the path through a forest is one that, when followed, gets you to the house. Truth, he said, *happens* to an idea; it becomes true, is made true, by events.

Then came the phrases that got him into trouble. James spoke of the "cash-value" of an idea in experiential terms, and wrote that the true is only the expedient in our way of thinking, just as the right is only the expedient in our way of behaving. Critics heard: whatever is convenient to believe is true. Bertrand Russell (whom we meet properly on Day 69) attacked the view: it is often far easier, he argued, to find out whether a belief is true than to find out whether believing it has good effects on the whole, so usefulness cannot be what truth means. James protested that he was misread; he meant "expedient in the long run and on the whole," taking all experience into account, not useful in the moment. Whether that defense works is still debated.

James's philosophy had a personal root. In his late twenties he suffered a severe depression, partly from fear that a scientific, deterministic universe left no room for human freedom. In April 1870 he wrote in his diary that, after reading the French philosopher Charles Renouvier, he resolved that his first act of free will would be to believe in free will. He chose the belief that let him live, and it worked. That experience shaped his most controversial essay.

sections.heading: The Will to Believe
sections.body:
In 1877 the English mathematician W.K. Clifford published "The Ethics of Belief." He told of a shipowner who sends an old, unseaworthy emigrant ship to sea. He suppresses his doubts, sincerely persuades himself that the ship is safe, and collects the insurance when it sinks. Clifford argued that the shipowner is guilty even though he sincerely believed, because he had no right to believe on such evidence. His conclusion became famous: "It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence."

James replied in "The Will to Believe" (1896). He agreed that in most matters we should follow the evidence. But he argued there are special cases where the evidence cannot decide and yet we must choose. He called these **genuine options**, and they have three features:

- **Living**: both possibilities are real candidates for you. (Becoming a Muslim might be a live option for one person and a dead one for another.)
- **Forced**: there is no third way; refusing to decide is itself a decision.
- **Momentous**: the stakes are high, the opportunity unique, the decision hard to reverse.

In such cases, James argued, our "passional nature" may lawfully decide. Clifford's rule says: better to risk missing the truth than to risk believing an error. James replies that this is itself a choice driven by a feeling, namely fear of being duped. Why should that feeling outrank hope?

James's best examples involve beliefs that help make themselves true. Will this person like me? If I wait for proof before acting warmly, I may never get it; my trust may create the friendship. A climber trapped on a mountain who must leap a chasm will jump farther if she believes she can. And religion, James argued, might be like this: if religious faith is a genuine option for you, Clifford's rule would forbid you from ever finding out whether it is true. Compare Kierkegaard's leap (Day 64), made in a far calmer key.

Critics, then and now, worry that James opens the door to wishful thinking. Couldn't a conspiracy theorist say his belief is "living, forced and momentous"? James's defenders reply that he set strict conditions: the matter must be one that evidence genuinely cannot settle, which is rarely the case for factual claims about the world.

sections.heading: John Dewey: Learning by Doing, Democracy as a Way of Life
sections.body:
John Dewey (1859–1952), born in Burlington, Vermont, in the year *Origin of Species* appeared, became the most publicly influential of the pragmatists. Early in his career he was a follower of Hegel (Day 59), and he kept Hegel's sense that mind and society develop over time. But Darwin taught him to see thinking as a natural activity of an organism coping with its environment. He called his version of pragmatism **instrumentalism**: ideas are tools for solving problems, to be judged by how well they work, much as we judge a hammer.

For Dewey, inquiry begins when a situation becomes problematic: our habits stop working and we feel stuck. We define the problem, form a hypothesis, try it out and see what happens. Philosophy's job is not to discover eternal truths beyond experience, a "quest for certainty" he thought had misled philosophers since Plato, but to help people think intelligently about the problems they actually face.

This view transformed education. In 1896 Dewey opened the Laboratory School at the University of Chicago, where children learned arithmetic by cooking and measuring, and history by building and weaving as earlier peoples had. The slogan "learning by doing" is associated with him, though the idea is older. In *Democracy and Education* (1916) he argued that education is not preparation for life but part of life itself, and that schools should be small democratic communities where children learn to cooperate, experiment and think for themselves rather than memorize and obey.

Democracy was Dewey's lifelong theme. He wrote in *Democracy and Education*: "A democracy is more than a form of government; it is primarily a mode of associated living, of conjoint communicated experience." Voting is not enough; democracy needs citizens who can inquire together, communicate freely and revise their views in light of results. Dewey practiced what he preached. He helped found the American Association of University Professors and the American Civil Liberties Union, was a friend of the social reformer Jane Addams, whose Hull House settlement in Chicago he admired, and at the age of seventy-seven traveled to Mexico in 1937 to chair a commission investigating Stalin's charges against Leon Trotsky. The commission found Trotsky not guilty.

sections.heading: Objections and the Pragmatist Legacy
sections.body:
Pragmatism has faced three major objections.

The first is the one Russell pressed: it seems to confuse **truth** with **usefulness**. Plenty of falsehoods are useful (a comforting lie, a convenient myth), and plenty of truths are painful or useless. If "true" just means "works," we lose the ability to say that a belief works *because* it is true. Peirce's version, truth as what inquiry would finally agree on, avoids the crudest form of this charge, which is one reason he distanced himself from James.

The second is that the pragmatic maxim may be too blunt. Some meaningful questions seem to have no practical consequences we could ever test, for instance questions about the distant past that has left no traces. The logical positivists (Day 71) would push a cousin of Peirce's maxim to a radical extreme, declaring untestable statements literally meaningless, and run into serious trouble.

The third is political. Critics on the left and right charged that pragmatism was a philosophy of American business: whatever succeeds is good. Dewey answered that "what works" always means what works to solve a shared problem, tested publicly and judged by its consequences for everyone affected. But critics notice that pragmatism tends to be vague about which goals are worth pursuing in the first place.

After Dewey's death, analytic philosophy, with its focus on logic and language (Days 69–74), dominated American universities and pragmatism looked old-fashioned. Yet its ideas kept surfacing. Quine (Day 74) described our knowledge as a web of belief revised as a whole in the face of experience, a very pragmatist picture. Popper's fallibilism (Day 72) echoes Peirce. And from the 1970s Richard Rorty, Hilary Putnam and Cornel West revived pragmatism by name. Not bad for a philosophy that began with a squirrel.

keyQuote.text: Consider what effects, that might conceivably have practical bearings, we conceive the object of our conception to have. Then, our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object.
keyQuote.source: Charles Sanders Peirce, 'How to Make Our Ideas Clear' (1878)

modernConnection.title: "Show Me the Data": Pragmatism in the Age of Experiments
modernConnection.body:
If you work in tech, medicine or public policy, you live in a pragmatist world without knowing it. A software company that cannot decide whether a green or blue button is better does not hold a philosophical debate; it runs an A/B test, showing each version to thousands of users and measuring what happens. Evidence-based medicine judges a treatment not by how elegant its theory sounds but by what randomized trials show it does for patients. "Evidence-based policy" asks whether a job-training scheme actually raises incomes. Peirce would recognize all of this as the method of science: settling belief by consequences that anyone can check, and staying ready to revise.

Dewey's influence is just as visible in classrooms. Project-based learning, science fairs, student councils and the idea that children should investigate rather than merely memorize all draw on his Laboratory School, even when teachers have never read him.

Even James's will to believe has a modern echo. Research on self-fulfilling expectations, such as studies suggesting that a teacher's expectations can affect students' progress, or that confidence can improve performance, fits his point that some beliefs help make themselves true. Coaches and therapists rely on it constantly.

But the comparison also shows pragmatism's weak spots. An A/B test can tell you which button gets more clicks; it cannot tell you whether more clicks is a good goal. Platforms that optimized relentlessly for "what works" (engagement) sometimes ended up rewarding outrage and misinformation. That is exactly the gap critics found in pragmatism: it is brilliant at choosing means and vaguer about choosing ends. Dewey would answer that ends, too, must be tested by their consequences for everyone affected, not just the company's metrics. And the self-fulfilling belief literature is a warning as well as an inspiration: several famous findings have proved hard to replicate. A good pragmatist would treat that, too, as a result worth learning from.

vocabulary.definition: The American philosophical movement holding that the meaning and value of ideas lie in their practical consequences for experience and action.
vocabulary.example: Asked whether two rival theories really differ, a pragmatist asks what different results we would observe if one or the other were true.

vocabulary.definition: The nineteenth-century New England movement led by Emerson and Thoreau that emphasized intuition, nature, self-reliance and individual conscience.
vocabulary.example: Thoreau's experiment at Walden Pond put Transcendentalism's ideal of simple, self-reliant living into practice.

vocabulary.definition: Peirce's rule that our idea of something consists entirely of our idea of its conceivable practical effects.
vocabulary.example: By the pragmatic maxim, calling a diamond 'hard' means that most other substances will not scratch it.

vocabulary.definition: The view that any of our beliefs, even well-supported scientific ones, might turn out to be mistaken and should remain open to revision.
vocabulary.example: A fallibilist scientist holds her best theory firmly but would abandon it if the evidence turned against it.

vocabulary.definition: In James, a choice between hypotheses that is living, forced and momentous, where he argued our passions may legitimately decide when evidence cannot.
vocabulary.example: For James, whether to embrace religious faith could be a genuine option for someone to whom both belief and unbelief seemed real possibilities.

vocabulary.definition: Dewey's version of pragmatism, which treats ideas and theories as tools for solving problems, judged by how well they work.
vocabulary.example: An instrumentalist judges a theory of education by how well students actually learn under it.

vocabulary.definition: The traditional view that a belief is true when it matches or corresponds to how reality actually is.
vocabulary.example: The correspondence theory says 'snow is white' is true just because snow is white; James asked what that agreement amounts to in practice.

thinkingExercise.title: The Squirrel Test
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use the pragmatic maxim as a tool on real disagreements. Spend 10 to 15 minutes on these steps, writing short answers.
steps: Pick a disagreement you have recently witnessed or taken part in (for example, whether a hot dog is a sandwich, whether a friend is 'lazy,' or whether a political policy is 'socialist').
Apply the pragmatic maxim: list what practical, observable differences it would make if each side were right. Do the two sides actually predict different things?
Decide: is this a real disagreement about facts, a verbal dispute like the squirrel case, or a disagreement about values? What would settle it?

Now test James: think of one belief you hold partly because it helps you live (about yourself, other people or the world). Is it a genuine option in his sense (living, forced, momentous), or are you just avoiding evidence?
Write a short paragraph: would Clifford condemn your belief? Who has the better argument in your case?

summary: Emerson and Thoreau's Transcendentalism gave America a philosophy of self-reliance and conscience; the pragmatists kept its independence but replaced intuition with experimental method and Darwinian thinking.
Peirce's pragmatic maxim says the meaning of an idea lies in its conceivable practical effects; he defended fallibilism and the method of science as the best way to fix belief.
James extended pragmatism to truth itself (true ideas are those that lead us successfully through experience) and argued that for genuine options our passions may decide when evidence cannot.
Dewey's instrumentalism treated ideas as tools for solving problems and inspired progressive education and a vision of democracy as a way of shared, inquiring life.
Critics charge that pragmatism confuses truth with usefulness and says too little about which ends are worth pursuing, yet its ideas resurfaced in Quine, Popper and the neopragmatists.

quiz.question: What does Peirce's pragmatic maxim tell us to do when trying to clarify an idea?
options: Trace the idea back to its historical origins
Ask what conceivable practical effects the idea's object would have
Check whether the idea is clear and distinct to reason
Ask whether believing the idea makes us happy
quiz.explanation: For Peirce, our conception of an object's practical effects is the whole of our conception of it. Genealogy, Cartesian clarity and happiness are not his test.

quiz.question: Thoreau argued, like Socrates in the Crito, that a citizen must obey the laws even when they are unjust.
quiz.explanation: Thoreau went to jail rather than pay a tax supporting slavery and war; for him conscience came before the law.

quiz.question: Which of Peirce's four methods of fixing belief lets beliefs be settled by an external reality through tests anyone can repeat?
options: Tenacity
Authority
The a priori method
Science
quiz.explanation: Only the method of science lets something outside us determine belief, so only it can correct its own errors.

quiz.question: How does James resolve the squirrel dispute?
options: By showing the answer depends on what we practically mean by 'going round,' so the dispute is verbal
By proving the man does go round the squirrel
By proving the man does not go round the squirrel
By declaring the question meaningless because it is about animals
quiz.explanation: Once the two practical meanings of 'going round' are distinguished, nothing is left to dispute.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three features of a 'genuine option' in James's 'The Will to Believe'?
options: Living
Forced
Provable
Momentous
quiz.explanation: A genuine option is living, forced and momentous. James's point is precisely that such options cannot be settled by proof or evidence.

quiz.question: W.K. Clifford argued that it is wrong always, everywhere and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.
quiz.explanation: This is the famous conclusion of 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877), illustrated by the shipowner who sincerely but wrongly believed his ship was safe.

quiz.question: A city tries a new bus route for six months, measures ridership and commute times, and then keeps or revises the plan based on results. Whose view of inquiry does this best illustrate?
options: Emerson's reliance on intuition
Clifford's ethics of belief
Kierkegaard's leap of faith
Dewey's instrumentalism
quiz.explanation: Dewey treated ideas as tools tested by how well they solve a problematic situation, revised in light of consequences.

quiz.question: What is the most common objection to James's theory of truth?
options: It makes truth depend on God's will
It seems to confuse being true with being useful or convenient to believe
It denies that experience has anything to do with truth
It holds that only mathematical statements can be true
quiz.explanation: Russell and others argued that useful falsehoods and useless truths show 'true' cannot simply mean 'works.'

quiz.question: Dewey believed democracy is mainly a matter of holding elections and has little to do with education.
quiz.explanation: Dewey called democracy 'primarily a mode of associated living' and saw schools as places to cultivate democratic, inquiring citizens.

quiz.question: Why did Peirce rename his own view 'pragmaticism'?
options: To distance it from the popularized version associated with James and others
Because the Metaphysical Club voted on the name
Because Dewey had trademarked the word 'pragmatism'
To show that he had abandoned the pragmatic maxim
quiz.explanation: Peirce disliked how pragmatism was being used and chose a name, he said, ugly enough to be safe from kidnappers.

goDeeper.body:
The deepest disagreement among the pragmatists concerns truth. Peirce defined it as the opinion inquiry would converge on in the long run, an ideal limit that makes truth independent of what any particular person finds convenient. James's language of truth 'happening' to ideas sounds far more personal and present-tense, which is why Russell, G.E. Moore and others accused him of subjectivism. Dewey largely avoided the word 'truth,' preferring 'warranted assertibility': a claim is warranted when it has been well tested by inquiry so far.

In the late twentieth century, Richard Rorty pushed James and Dewey in a radical direction. In *Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature* (1979) he argued that the whole project of showing how the mind 'mirrors' reality was a mistake, and that we should stop asking whether our beliefs correspond to the world and instead ask whether they help us cope and converse. Truth, on his provocative view, is what our peers will let us get away with saying. Hilary Putnam, Susan Haack and Cheryl Misak pushed back, defending a Peircean pragmatism that keeps truth as a real goal of inquiry. Misak argues that Rorty abandoned what was best in the tradition.

A second fruitful thread is pragmatism's connection to social reform. Jane Addams, often left out of histories of philosophy, developed pragmatist ideas through her work at Hull House, arguing that ethics must be learned from contact with the lives of the poor and immigrants. Cornel West's *The American Evasion of Philosophy* (1989) reads the tradition, from Emerson to Du Bois, as 'prophetic pragmatism,' a philosophy aimed at democratic struggle rather than abstract theory.

questions: Can a belief be useful to hold but false? If so, what does that show about James's theory of truth?
Is Clifford right that believing on insufficient evidence is always wrong, or are there cases where James's will to believe applies?
Is pragmatism good at choosing means but unable to choose ends? How might Dewey reply?
